extracted.intended_audience: general readers of history/biography; students of political/intellectual history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative statements and descriptive standards embedded in a 19th-century historical/biographical essay about statesmen, rhetoric, and education. The passage offers qualities used to judge statesmen, their policy style, eloquence, and educational expectations in the Tudor–Elizabethan period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statesman temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: They proceeded, not with the impetuosity of theologians, but with the calm determination of statesmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They acted, not like men who considered the Romish worship as a system too offensive to God, and too destructive of souls, to be tolerated for an hour, but like men who regarded the points in dispute among Christians as in themselves unimportant, and who were not restrained by any scruple of conscience from professing... They took a deliberate view of the state of their own country and of the Continent: they satisfied themselves as to the leaning of the public mind; and they chose their side. They placed themselves at the head of the Protestants of Europe, and staked all their fame and fortunes on the success of their party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Their policy was generally characterised rather by vigilance, by moderation, and by firmness, than by invention, or by the spirit of enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No particular faculty was pre-eminently developed; but manly health and vigour were equally diffused through the whole. In active life, however, no men could be more perfectly free from the faults of mere theorists and pedants. No men observed more accurately the signs of the times. No men had a greater practical acquaintance with human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eloquence and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Their eloquence was less copious and less ingenious, but far purer and more manly... luminous, dignified, solid, and very slightly tainted with that affectation which deformed the style of the ablest men of the next age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If, as sometimes chanced, these politicians were under the necessity of taking a part in the theological controversies... they acquitted themselves as if their whole lives had been passed in the Schools and the Convocation. Their speeches exhibited compactness of expression and a richness of illustration drawn from literature and history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability, moderation, and avoidance of ostentation
rubrics_metrics.description: They were more solicitous to lay the foundations of their power deep than to raise the structure to a conspicuous but insecure height (motto: Mediocria firma).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: None of them aspired to be sole Minister. None of them provoked envy by an ostentatious display of wealth and influence. None of them affected to outshine the ancient aristocracy of the kingdom. Only one was made a peer; and he was content with the lowest degree of the peerage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private morals and household governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Their fidelity to the State was incorruptible. Their private morals were without stain. Their households were sober and well governed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As to money, none of them could, in that age, justly be considered as rapacious. Some of them would, even in our time, deserve the praise of eminent disinterestedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical education as historical necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: In the time of Henry the Eighth and Edward the Sixth, a person who did not read Greek and Latin could read nothing, or next to nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Latin was the language of courts as well as of the schools. It was the language of diplomacy; it was the language of theological and political controversy. Being ignorant of it shut one out from acquaintance with political, literary, and religious discourse of the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative value of ancient versus modern literatures
rubrics_metrics.description: The books which have been written in the languages of western Europe, during the last two hundred and fifty years... are of greater value than all the books which at the beginning of that period were extant in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though the great productions of Athenian and Roman genius remain of high positive value, their relative value has declined as the modern languages and literatures have grown. Modern readers can often compensate for lack of classical knowledge with contemporary works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary oratorical method
rubrics_metrics.description: He dealt with every great question, not in small detached portions, but as a whole; he refined little, and his reasonings were those of a capacious rather than a subtle mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ben Jonson praised Bacon's speaking as 'neatly, more pressly, more weightily, or suffered less emptiness, less idleness, in what he uttered.' His speeches were compact, full of apt illustrations, and commanded the attention of his hearers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnosis of factional motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Both parties employed the means which are familiar to unscrupulous statesmen; and neither had, or even pretended to have, any important end in view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the close of Elizabeth's reign factions differed on no important public question: both belonged to the Established Church, professed loyalty, approved the war with Spain; the quarrel was largely over shares of power and patronage rather than principle.
